title: Loops
summary: Repeat work with for and while loops, plus break and continue.

checkpoints.title: for and while
checkpoints.content: `for item in range(5):` runs its block once for each value 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — `range(5)` never includes 5 itself. `while condition:` repeats as long as the condition stays true, so you need something inside the loop that eventually makes it false, or it never stops.
checkpoints.explanation: range(n) always starts at 0 and stops one short of n, giving exactly n values — the same off-by-one pattern as slicing.

hints.H0: range(5) produces 5 numbers, but the last one is 4, not 5.
hints.H1: A while loop needs its condition to eventually become false.
hints.H2: for loops over range() are for a known number of repeats; while is for an unknown number.

checkpoints.title: Predict a for loop
checkpoints.content: How many times does the block inside `for i in range(3, 7):` run?

options.explanation: range(3, 7) starts at 3 and stops before 7, producing 3, 4, 5, 6 — four values.
range(3, 7) doesn't start counting from 0 or run 7 times — it starts at 3 and stops before 7.
That would be range(3) — passing two arguments changes the start point to 3.

checkpoints.explanation: With two arguments, range(start, stop) begins at start and produces values up to (but not including) stop.

hints.H0: range with two arguments doesn't start at 0.
hints.H1: List out the values: 3, 4, 5, 6 — does 7 appear?

checkpoints.title: Write a range() call
checkpoints.content: Write a `range(...)` call that produces exactly the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
checkpoints.explanation: To include 5 as the last value, the stop argument must be one more than 5, since range's stop is exclusive.

hints.H0: range's stop value is never included in the result.
hints.H1: You want the last number produced to be 5.

checkpoints.title: break vs continue
checkpoints.content: Inside a loop, what does `continue` do, compared to `break`?

options.text: continue skips to the next iteration; break exits the loop entirely.
options.explanation: continue jumps back to the top of the loop for the next item; break stops the loop immediately, even if items remain.

options.text: continue exits the loop entirely; break skips to the next iteration.
options.explanation: That's backwards — break is the one that exits, continue is the one that skips ahead.

options.text: They do the same thing — either can be used interchangeably.
options.explanation: They have distinctly different effects: one exits the whole loop, the other just moves to the next item.

checkpoints.explanation: continue moves on to the loop's next iteration, skipping the rest of the current one; break stops the loop altogether, running nothing more inside it.

hints.H0: One of these keywords ends the loop completely.
hints.H1: The other just skips the remainder of the current pass.
